# Samathakkhandhaka (Kd 14)

**ID:** Kd 14
**Section:** Khandhaka (kd)
**Collection:** Vinaya
**Title (Pali):** Samathakkhandhaka
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** The chapter on the settling of legal issues
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/pli-tv-kd14
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/vin02m3.mul3.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Samathakkhandhaka* (Kd 14, comprising chapter IV of the *Cullavagga*) provides an extensive exposition of the procedures for resolving monastic legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*) [SuttaCentral; von Hinüber 1996; Prebish 1994]. It articulates how the seven rules for settling legal disputes (*adhikaraṇasamathadhamma*) found at the end of the Pātimokkha are implemented in monastic practice, and provides a technical analysis of the four classes of legal issues (*vivādādhikaraṇa*, *anuvādādhikaraṇa*, *āpattādhikaraṇa*, and *kiccādhikaraṇa*) [SuttaCentral; Vinayamukha 1983; Prebish 1994]. Scholars have highlighted its internal structural format, noting the presence of an early *mātṛkā* style that organizes disputes into categories such as right, wrong, and undetermined [Sung 1999]. In terms of relative chronology, Oskar von Hinüber notes that the text is familiar with the *Suttavibhaṅga* [von Hinüber 1996].

Substantively, the text details various formal ecclesiastical acts (*kamma*) and settlement mechanisms. These include the verdict in the presence of the assembly and the Dhamma (*sammukhavinaya*), the verdict of innocence based on recollection (*smṛtivinaya*), the verdict regarding an unrepented offense (*tassapāpiyasikākamma*), settlement through collective confession as if "covering with grass" (*tiṇavatthāraka*), and resolution upon acknowledgment (*pratijñākāraka*) [Vinayamukha 1983; Prebish 1994; Prebish 1996].

Full cross-sectarian parallels exist across monastic traditions, notably the *Adhikaraṇavastu* (or *Śamathavastu*) preserved in Sanskrit fragments and Tibetan translation, as well as Chinese Vinaya versions across the Mūlasarvāstivāda, Sarvāstivāda, Dharmaguptaka, and Mahīśāsaka lineages [SuttaCentral; Härtel 1956; Banerjee 1979; Prebish 1994]. Sutta-level parallels treating the same settlement principles include the *Sāmagāma Sutta* (MN 104) and the *Saṅgīti Sutta* (DN 33) [SuttaCentral; Prebish 1996]. Text-reuse data computed by DharmaNexus confirms extensive alignment between Kd 14 and MN 104 (§14.29.8–14.29.29 ↔ §19.3–19.23 with 94% similarity), as well as widespread internal reuse with the *Parivāra* (particularly *Samathabheda* [Pvr 5] and *Adhikaraṇabheda* [Pvr 11]), and with other Khandhaka chapters such as the *Kammakkhandhaka* (Kd 11) and *Samuccayakkhandhaka* (Kd 13) [DharmaNexus].
